description.narrative:
Financial Sector Deepening Program (FSDK) finansieras gemensamt av flera givare och verkar i Kenya via en stiftelse, eller Trust. FSDK etablerades för att befrämja en utveckling av finanssektorn samt för öka fattiga människors tillgång till finansiella tjänster i Kenya. FSDK:s strategimål för 2016-2021 är att "åstadkomma varaktiga förbättringar av kenyanska låginkomsttagares levnadsförhållanden". I detta ingår att hitta möjligheter att skapa resiliens, hållbarhet och förbättrade levnadsförhållanden för låginkomsttagare. Det specifika målet är att "utveckla ett finansiellt system som skapar ett verkligt värde för låginkomsttagare i Kenya". Detta ska ske genom att samarbeta med marknadsaktörer i syfte att undanröja de hinder som finns för ett inkluderande system: 1. Hög kostnad; 2. otillräckligt värde; och 3. lågt förtroende. För att åstadkomma detta vill man bygga upp kapacitet hos aktörerna så att de kan arbeta för att undanröja hinder och hitta innovativa lösningar som kommer fattiga människor och företag till del. I detta ingår att: ändra spelreglerna och öka incitamenten för att gynna fattiga; förbättra effektiviteten inom branschen; samt befrämja en samsyn om finanssektorns utveckling.
Den reviderade budgeten, efter att DFID avbrutit sitt stöd till programmet Financial Inclusion, uppgår till 3,188 miljarder KES, varav 1,622 miljarder KES redan säkrats av Gates Foundation och 1,086 miljarder KES överförts från tidigare strategistöd (i januari 2017). Sverige ombeds bidra med 0,48 miljarder KES (50 MSEK).

The Financial Sector Deepening (FSDK) Program is a multi-donor programme operating in Kenya through a Trust association modality. FSDK was established to facilitate the development of the financial sector and to increase the access for poor people to financial services in Kenya. FSDK Strategy 2016-2021 goal is “to generate sustainable improvements in the lives of lower-income people in Kenya” which entail seeking opportunities which build resilience, growth and improvement in quality of life for the low-income Groups. The specific objective is “to develop a financial system which delivers real value to the low-income people in Kenya”. This will be articulated through working with market players to address three key barriers to inclusion including: 1. High cost; 2. Insufficient value; and 3. Weak trust. Key approach to attainment of this is building capacity for the market to address market barriers and innovate solutions for real world needs of poor people and businesses by addressing market challenges (outcomes) which include: rules of the game (which shift incentives in favour of the poor); enhancing efficiencies in the industry infrastructure; and promoting a shared collective vision on development of the Financial Services Sector.
The revised budgetary requirement following DFID exit from support to core Financial Inclusion programme is BKES 3.188 out of which BKES 1.622 has already been secured from Gates Foundation and BKES 1.086 is a carryover from previous strategy support (as at January 2017). Sweden is requested to provide BKES 0.48 (MSEK 50).

The intervention has two components namely financial inclusion and trade facilitation. The intended outcome is to generate sustainable improvements in the lives of lower-income people in Kenya through development of a financial and trade system which delivers real value to the low-income people in Kenya. The objectives of this intervention; both financial inclusion and trade facilitation is anchored on working with market players to address three key bariers to inclusion namely i) high cost;ii) insufficient value; and iii) weak trust in the system While the specific approach to attainment of these objectives of reducing costs, creating value and building trust in both the financial and trade market system relies on building the capacity of the market to work with key areas including: rules of the game which shift incentives in favour of the poor; enhancing efficiencies in the industry infrastructure; and promoting a shared collective vision on development of the financial services sector (FSS). Additionally, trade facilitation for the real economy aims at creating market capacity and incentives to innovate trade solutions which deliver real value for the economy, enterprises and households. The rationale behind the trade facilitation is that the trade system must evolve in a way that it only allocates value to trading partners in line with the value they have added within the system and by breaking down information asymmetries.

description.narrative:
Sida has a core support with FSDK that included the following projects.
Green finance project implements a comprehensive strategy encompassing policy and regulatory strengthening, technical assistance, market driven engagements, and the enhancement of climate data capabilities. The project has been supporting four counties (Nairobi, Mombasa, Kirinyaga and Kiambu) deepen their Climate Change Capacity Fund (CCCF) mechanism as an enabler of local climate actions. FSD assessed the potential for 10 counties (Wajir, Taita Taveta, Embu, Laikipia, Makueni, Kisumu, Vihiga, Nairobi, Nandi and Kirinyaga) to access and apply to the bond market for the development of green activities.
The county green finance assessment was the first of its kind in the country and has generated actionable insights on what the potential, opportunities and challenges exist at county level in terms of the financing of green projects and assets. County green finance assessment demonstrates the green finance opportunity at county level in Kenya Financial Sector Deepening Kenya.
Agriculture and processing project builds and strengthens partnerships that support access to inputs, know how and mechanization, enhance green resilience as well as broaden access to better output markets for smallholder women farmers and processors. FSD convened, curated, and participated in select sessions of the Financing Agriculture Sustainably (FINAS) 2024 conference. In collaboration with AGRA, FSD made a case for one focal point for Agricultural finance in Kenya which explored what an agricultural finance coordination unit would mean and look like for Kenya.
Another session was also curated by FSD highlighted the challenges in coordinating smallholders and implications for finance as showcased by various models. FSD Kenya at the Financing Agriculture Sustainably Conference (FINAS 2024).
Health finance project facilitates and advocates for value adding finance that enables improved health and financial resilience to health shocks for women and households. Under the financial solutions to help women and households to deal with health shocks component, FSD designed the maternal and neonatal health (MNH) valuebased care (VBC) programme. The package of care to be provided to mothers and new borns under Britams Afya Tele insurance cover was defined. A key part of this pilot is the need to send the right nudges to the expectant mothers to drive the right behavior and promote the desired health outcomes. Britam and FSD Kenyas valuebased care maternal and neonatal health pilot program to reduce costs and improve health outcomes
Affordable housing project builds on existing partnerships to explore a healthy pipeline of additional work to influence affordable housing policy and increase access to wellbeing goods and services. Given the assent of the 2023 Housing Bill into an Act on 19th March 2024, FSDs intends to support State Department of Housing and Urban Development (SDHUD) with data collection and analysis on 20 projects across Kenya. In this effort, FSD hosted a successful twoday workshop in February 2024, which garnered deep participation from several departments of State Department of. Housing and Urban Development (SDHUD) , National Housing Corporation, National Construction Authority, and Centre for Affordable Housing Finance (CAHF)
Policy and Infrastructure project focusses on enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of the infrastructure that underpins Kenyas payments and credit markets and supports the development of an enabling environment for green finance, agriculture and rural finance and an inclusive digital economy through the implementation of the MediumTerm Plan 4 (MTP4) and other policy reform processes.
Crosscutting support from the Thought leadership functions: Research focuses primarily on supporting the FinAccess survey and ensuring that the results of the surveys continue to inform inclusive financial sector development. This support ensures better capture of the drivers and impacts of inclusive finance, including climate risk, finance for farmers, MSEs and women, health finance, finance for affordable housing, etc.
FinAccess Household Surveys. The surveys have taken place in 2006, 2009, 2013, 2016, 2019,2021 and the latest in 2024. The Surveys were initiated to enhance financial inclusion measurement provide better understanding of the financial inclusion landscape indicators to track financial inclusion dynamics over time and data to various stakeholders. The financial inclusion measurement cuts across the four dimensions of: Access, Usage, Quality and Impact/ Welfare. Results from the survey are crucial in shaping financial decisions by the Central bank of Kenya.
The surveys have informed various policy and industry initiatives such as agency banking regulations, improved consumer protection measures, influenced Vision 2030 medium term plans tracking, supported innovations such as informing MTiba and MShwari, which address the needs of underserved populations. The data has also highlighted irresponsible practices like predatory lending and gambling, prompting corrective measures
The partnership with FSD comes to an end in September 2025 and will not be renewed.
